title: Why Piki Lopez is letting Rockwell go
summary: The Rockwell sale accomplishes something months of Lopez family boardroom battles couldn't

blocks.text: Part 1 | The Lopez heirs who ran Rockwell but never controlled itPart 2 | Why Gabby Lopez wants Rockwell as ABS-CBN struggles
Federico “Piki” Lopez is selling a business that is making money. And the buyer is his cousin Eugenio “Gabby” Lopez III, one of the loudest critics of his leadership.

Rockwell Land, the property developer behind Power Plant Mall and Alabang Town Center, earned about P3.79 billion in profit in the first nine months of 2026, up 21.5% from a year earlier. Yet on November 12, the board of First Philippine Holdings Corporation (FPH), chaired by Piki, approved selling its controlling stake in Rockwell to Crème Investment Corporation, the private holding firm of Gabby and siblings, for P15.92 billion.
A company doesn’t have to be failing to be sold. Sometimes the controlling owner simply wants to put the money somewhere else.

In Piki’s case, the decision also follows months of open warfare among the third-generation Lopez cousins over who should run the family empire. Last year, First Gen sold control of its natural gas business to Prime Infrastructure in a deal worth about P48.8 billion. This year, it rejected an Indonesian investor’s offer valuing geothermal producer Energy Development Corporation (EDC) at US$5 billion. Meanwhile, FPH has spent billions buying back its own shares while keeping regular dividends flat.
Piki is keeping the energy business a foreign buyer wants, while letting go of a profitable developer his cousins want to own.

The sale solves two problems at once: it hands FPH extra cash for capital-hungry power projects, and it moves Rockwell, long tied to the late Manuel “Manolo” Lopez and his children, out of Piki’s corporate structure. Still, FPH has public shareholders who didn’t sign up to fund a family truce. For them, the only question that matters is whether selling Rockwell makes financial sense, no matter what it fixes among the cousins.
Rockwell and FPH’s power businesses have very different timelines, but both eat up huge amounts of money.

Rockwell’s P21.6-billion purchase of Alabang Commercial Corporation comes with installment payments running through December 2027, and its project spending hit roughly P9.5 billion in the first nine months of 2026. Meanwhile, First Gen and EDC are pouring billions into geothermal drilling, renewable energy, battery storage, and hydropower. First Gen’s Wawa and Pakil pumped-storage projects require heavy funding through 2029, with commercial operations targeted around 2030 and big profits expected starting in 2031.

As First Gen President and COO Giles Puno told shareholders in May 2026, “Beginning in 2031, these facilities are projected to contribute approximately P16 billion annually to First Gen’s bottom line, through a 20-year contracted agreement under the Department of Energy’s Green Energy Auction Program.” That is a massive future income stream. But it requires billions in investment years before the cash rolls in. (READ: From ‘king’ to ‘steward’: How Piki Lopez answered the Lopez family rift question)

Pumped-storage facilities use electricity to pump water uphill when power is cheap, then release it to generate electricity when demand spikes. They help stabilize a power grid relying more on renewables, but they are expensive and slow to build. Geothermal exploration is risky, too: companies must spend heavily to drill for underground steam before knowing how much power a site can actually produce.

blocks.caption: Diagram of the 1400 MW Pakil Pumped-storage Hydroelectric Power Project in Pakil, Laguna. Image from Ahunan Power Environmental Impact Statement

blocks.text: Piki has repeatedly built his strategy around the long-term payoff of patient bets, preaching “direction over speed” in his 2026 speeches. In the power business, patience isn’t optional. Selling Rockwell removes one hungry business competing for cash while giving FPH money to spend elsewhere.

The deal also clears Rockwell’s debt off FPH’s combined balance sheet once the developer is no longer a subsidiary. Rockwell carried more than P52 billion in total debt. Still, moving debt off the books isn’t the same as paying it off. And FPH is also giving up Rockwell’s entire property business, including its future earnings and obligations, for cash.

Piki’s strategy becomes much clearer when compared against two energy offers he turned down this year. In July, Barito Renewables Energy, linked to Indonesian billionaire Prajogo Pangestu, made an unsolicited offer valuing EDC’s equity at about US$5 billion (and up to US$7 billion including debt). First Gen said no. In September, its officials said they had no plans to sell EDC. Instead, in September, EDC teamed up with Indonesia’s Sinar Mas group to export its geothermal drilling know-how into Indonesia.

A month after Barito’s approach, parent company FPH also rejected a proposal from global private equity firm KKR to buy more shares in First Gen at P35 per share, a deal that would have handed FPH roughly P10.6 billion in cash. But KKR’s offer came with strings attached. Not just one, but three: it wanted FPH to sell shares at a discount while delisting First Gen from the stock exchange; it would have reduced FPH’s common stake before 50% while lifting KKR to roughly 40% under a new shareholders agreement; and it demanded strict tripwire requiring a mandatory buyout if control ever shifted at First Gen or any holding company above it. FPH said no again, arguing that P35 per share did “not reflect the company’s true value.” Sure enough, weeks later, KKR sold its First Gen stake to Singapore-based Gateway Partners’ Angana finance at P36 per share.

blocks.caption: Making sense of US firm KKR’s offer on Lopez family’s First Gen

blocks.text: Put those numbers side by side and the logic of the Rockwell sale becomes crystal clear. FPH refused to surrender EDC’s irreplaceable geothermal edge at any price, and refused to sell a slice of First Gen at a discount with governances strings attached. By selling Rockwell instead, FPH brings in P15.92 billion, roughly 50% more cash than KKR’s offer without giving up a single share of its core power business or handling an outside partner veto power over the group.

EDC isn’t just a collection of power plants. It owns steam fields, holds development rights, and has spent decades mastering how to find and manage underground geothermal energy. That kind of expertise is hard and expensive to copy. Keeping EDC protects both a steady business and specialized knowledge that can fuel expansion outside the Philippines.

blocks.caption: The company the Lopezes gave up Meralco for: EDC, from oil crisis child to takeover target

blocks.text: Rockwell is a different story. Its luxury condos, office leases, and malls make good money, but they sit outside the power and industrial core that increasingly defines FPH. That doesn’t make real estate less valuable. It just shows Piki values geothermal know-how more than owning malls and condos. For EDC, knowledge is worth more kept than sold. For Rockwell, FPH found its price.

FPH isn’t selling Rockwell because it is desperate for cash. In 2025, FPH reported roughly P19.8 billion in net income, including P15.1 billion in recurring profit. First Gen’s natural gas deal also brought major resources into the group (though that P48.8-billion deal value isn’t all sitting around as spendable cash). FPH already holds roughly P76 billion in consolidated cash and short-term financial assets. It also has P38.2 billion in appropriated retained earnings through December 2027—money earmarked for specific company plans, rather than a separate pile of spare cash.

The Rockwell sale will bring FPH P15.92 billion in gross proceeds once it closes. Management hasn’t earmarked it for any specific power project yet. Even so, it gives the company more breathing room to fund investments, pay down debt, or reward shareholders. It could also give FPH room to clean up its messy cross-ownership setup. Lopez Holdings owns 60.67% of FPH, while FPH owns 15.76% of Lopez Holdings, a loop that complicates how dividends flow between the two listed firms, though no plan to untangle it has been announced.

There is another practical perk to selling Rockwell instead of shaking up FPH or First Gen. Big ownership changes at the top companies can trigger expensive penalty clauses in loan and joint-venture contracts—including agreements with Prime Infrastructure and FPH’s lenders. Selling a subsidiary like Rockwell avoids setting off those costly triggers.

blocks.caption: Why everyone wants a piece of the Lopez group’s Energy Development Corp.

blocks.text: How FPH spends its money reveals a lot about Piki’s playbook. In 2025, FPH spent roughly P3.36 billion buying back its own shares, bringing total buybacks to about P13.11 billion by year-end. It later added another P5 billion to the buyback budget through September 2028.
Buybacks and dividends reward shareholders in very different ways:

items: Dividends hand cash directly to every stockholder based on how many shares they own.
Buybacks pay cash only to investors who sell their shares, which shrinks the share count and leaves remaining owners with a bigger slice of the company.

blocks.text: For the Lopez family, which already controls the holding company, ongoing buybacks quietly increase their ownership percentage as long as they don’t sell.

Meanwhile, FPH has kept its regular dividend frozen at P2.20 per share for five straight years, despite strong profits and big asset sales. First Gen even cut its annual dividend from P0.90 per share in 2024 to P0.80 in 2025, citing heavy capital spending and debt payments.

Holding onto cash gives management fuel for massive power projects. But it also puts pressure on Piki to prove that keeping the money beats handing it to investors. With another P15.92 billion coming in from Rockwell, shareholders will be asking: Will this cash go toward more buybacks, new power plants, debt cuts, or finally a bigger dividend?

FPH agreed to sell 5.3 billion Rockwell common shares (about 86.58% of the common stock) at P3 each, plus 2.75 billion voting preferred shares at P0.01 each. That brings the total price to roughly P15.92 billion and transfers 90.74% of the voting power.

In its November 13 disclosure to the Philippine Stock Exchange, FPH said it engaged BDO Capital & Investment Corporation which valued Rockwell’s common shares at P2.47 to P3.09 per share. The agreed price of P3 falls toward the upper end of that range. FPH said the price was determined through arm’s-length negotiations with Crème. That is a solid benchmark, though it doesn’t automatically prove FPH got the best price for a growing commercial developer.

Rockwell carries heavy debt, construction bills, and unpaid installments from its Alabang deal, all of which weigh on its price tag. On the flip side, it brings steady mall rent, a strong housing pipeline, and prime land. The real question is whether P15.92 billion fairly pays FPH for giving up all those future profits.

FPH noted that the deal was backed by BDO Capital’s independent valuation, reviewed by outside lawyers and independent directors, and still requires regulatory sign-off—including clearance from the Philippine Competition Commission and a mandatory buyout offer for Rockwell’s remaining public stockholders. Those guardrails matter, but investors still deserve to see how the price was negotiated and whether other buyers were ever considered.

The Rockwell sale accomplishes something months of boardroom battles couldn’t: it moves a business tied to Piki’s critics out of the empire he runs. Gabby Lopez and Manolo Lopez’s children challenged Piki’s leadership earlier this year. In September, Piki locked down control of the Lopez Holdings and FPH boards. Now, Gabby’s firm is buying Rockwell, the company long associated with Manolo’s side of the family. (READ: How to make yourself very expensive to fire: The Lopez cousins’ war)

Selling Rockwell could cool down future fights over management, dividends, and spending priorities. It also removes one of Piki’s loudest critics from FPH’s property business. Still, it doesn’t prove that Gabby has been silenced, that the cousins have buried the hatchet, or that the deal is part of a secret peace treaty.

For everyday public stockholders, the bigger issue is whether the deal was cut on fair terms. FPH noted that BDO Capital provided an independent valuation, and that independent directors and outside lawyers were involved. Even so, shareholders still deserve to know how the price was set, how conflicts of interest were handled, and whether FPH considered other buyers.
A deal that calms a family feud can certainly be good for business. But keeping peace in the family isn’t a good enough reason on its own for a public company to sell a profitable subsidiary.

blocks.text: Look at Piki’s moves over the past two years and a clear pattern emerges: First Gen sold control of its gas business, turned down a multibillion-dollar offer for EDC, and kept pouring money into renewable energy. FPH spent billions buying back shares while keeping regular dividends flat. Now, it is selling Rockwell for nearly P16 billion.

These deals leave Piki running a conglomerate focused heavily on power and industry, while Gabby’s branch walks away with a profitable property developer outside Piki’s reach. It may be a practical way to separate the cousins’ turf after months of fighting. At the same time, FPH is giving up a proven business with steady cash flow, prime properties, and strong future growth.

There is an argument for selling Rockwell that goes beyond the P15.92-billion price tag. Months of boardroom battles have eaten up time and energy that could have gone into running and growing the business. If the sale lets the cousins pursue their own goals without fighting over the same companies, Piki gains something valuable: the freedom to focus on his power and industrial businesses with fewer distractions and less uncertainty at the top. That kind of peace is hard to price, yet it can make a real difference to how a company runs.

There is an equally strong case for keeping Rockwell. It makes money, owns prime real estate, and could keep sending profits and dividends to FPH for years, cash that could help fund the group’s power projects without giving up a company that took decades to build. Selling Rockwell means trading all those future earnings for a fixed payout today. And while the cash is guaranteed, the peace isn’t. The cousins haven’t announced a formal settlement, and this deal won’t automatically end their disagreements.

Is peace worth it? That comes down to what FPH gains by letting Rockwell go versus what it loses by walking away. Keeping Rockwell brings steady profits and long-term upside. Selling it brings immediate cash, a tighter business focus, and a chance to end a costly family war. Both paths have real value, and both carry risks.

For Piki, the choice isn’t simply between peace and profit. It is a choice between two different futures for FPH: keeping Rockwell inside a diversified empire to generate steady cash alongside its power plants, or concentrating everything on energy and industry while the cousins go their separate ways.
The real question isn’t just whether peace is worth the price of Rockwell. It is whether FPH and its shareholders will be better off with Rockwell—or without it. – Rappler.com

Lala Rimando wrote about Philippine business, and managed newsrooms, including Newsbreak, ABS-CBN, Rappler, and Forbes, for over 25 years. She’s now based in La Union, taking care of her mom with dementia, and working on the multimedia biography of the late John Gokongwei.
